Title: Now that I have my notes... (Tournament rule 1.4)

Messages.Author: vol...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
This question never really came up before, because nobody really took
notes. The restrictions on them rendered them fairly pointless. Now
that I can take whatever notes I want, however, what are the
restrictions about what I DO with those notes?

Can I, for instance, gather notes from several of my friends and hand
them to the one player from our group who's in the final? If the
answer to this is no (because it would be considered outside coaching),
then where is that line drawn?

Example: In the Milwaukee GLQ, I decided to try taking notes, and I
definitely found that it would have helped me somewhat had I been in
the final. (For reference, I took notes not only of the things
happening at my table, but things I overheard across the room regarding
play at other tables.) I had a number of people asking if they could
look at my notes, which were open next to me. Was I obligated to hide
them? Or perhaps was I obligated to NOT hide them? Or am I free to do
with them whatever I choose, showing them to some people but not
others? If I am allowed to hand them to a Chicago player in the final,
does he have to show them to everyone?

If, by the way, I should not be sharing my notes, then how strict
should we be about between-round discussions? As far as I can tell,
the note-taking rule was relaxed because some people have better
short-term recall than others, and memory is not supposed to be a
critical factor in V:TES. So it seems to me that any rules that apply
to note-taking should apply to conversation as well.

-Eric Simon

None set by V:EKN rules (assuming you otherwise conform to V:EKN rules
-- no stalling, etc.)

> Can I, for instance, gather notes from several of my friends and hand
> them to the one player from our group who's in the final? If the
> answer to this is no (because it would be considered outside coaching),
> then where is that line drawn?
>
> Example: In the Milwaukee GLQ, I decided to try taking notes, and I
> definitely found that it would have helped me somewhat had I been in
> the final. (For reference, I took notes not only of the things
> happening at my table, but things I overheard across the room regarding
> play at other tables.) I had a number of people asking if they could
> look at my notes, which were open next to me. Was I obligated to hide
> them? Or perhaps was I obligated to NOT hide them? Or am I free to do
> with them whatever I choose, showing them to some people but not
> others? If I am allowed to hand them to a Chicago player in the final,
> does he have to show them to everyone?

You cannot discuss (including by notes) anything with the players of a
game you are not involved in. If you must (because you see some illegal
play, for instance), the do so through a judge. Or wait until the game
is finished.

> If, by the way, I should not be sharing my notes, then how strict
> should we be about between-round discussions? As far as I can tell,
> the note-taking rule was relaxed because some people have better
> short-term recall than others, and memory is not supposed to be a
> critical factor in V:TES.

Memory capability is not a factor to the creation of the tournament
rules, and the rule was not relaxed for any sort of "levelling the
playing field for memory-impaired" reasons.

Messages.Author: vol...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
Okay, so within my own game, I can show or not show players my notes as
I choose. What about during later rounds when those notes pertain to
previous games?

And was it illegal of me to take notes on things that I overheard
across the room during my game?

And does this mean that the between-round conversations about the
tables that inevitably happen are also illegal (though this has not
been strictly enforced)?

I ask these questions because written notes offer the possibility of
formalizing something illegal that is happening informally anyway.
However, I don't think that it's the formal nature of the activity that
makes it illegal, it's the fact that some players are getting
information from beyond their own games that is the problem. But this
happens all the time. My argument is this: if sharing notes beyond my
game is illegal, so is conversing about my table between rounds. If
we're not going to enforce the latter, why should the former be
enforced? Personally, I would rather we enforce both, but that creates
a very strict tournament environment that some may not enjoy.

-Eric Simon

There are tournament rules involving delay of game, and if someone's

write down "Joe is playing 8 deflections and 2 Delaying Tactics", why

Messages.Author: Matthew T. Morgan
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 14 May 2006 vol...@yahoo.com wrote:

> Woah. Really? Can I get some confirmation on this? So there is no
> problem with the original idea of having all the Chicago players take
> notes and then hand them to whichever one of us makes it to the final?
> Is that really where this is going?

I'm willing to guess that that is currently a legal (yet slimy) thing to
do simply because nobody has bothered to outlaw it. I see it as the sort
of rule we hope we don't need because nobody would do it anyway.

I mean, sure, the Chicago gang all contributes intel to its star. Other
players start targeting Chicago players in hopes of a Chi-free final, or
trying to deliberately feed them bad information in order to make the
intel network useless. That's not vtes. The game should be at the table.
More importantly, it's not a team game. I should be thinking "beat Eric"
when you're at my table, not "beat Chicago" if we're at the same
tournament.

Finally, the time between rounds at tournaments is for talking crap and
Duffin Drafting, not for having your army of nerds organize its notes!
Get your priorities straight!

If you were to start doing this kind of thing (and I'm guessing you were
only talking hypothetically anyway), I hope and expect there'd be a rule
against it pretty quickly.

Matt Morgan

> I'm willing to guess that that is currently a legal (yet slimy) thing to

> of rule we hope we don't need because nobody would do it anyway.

I'm not seeing how you could possibly rule against sharing intel like
this. Like, you could say "no transfering notes" or something, but you
can't stop people from talking when they go to get a sandwich, and I
could just tell you all pertinent information, and you could just take
note on what I tell you.

This is one of those deeply weird situations that you can't really do
anything about, and the best thing to do is just not worry about it.
Most people aren't going to bother to take notes, and even if they do,
and even if they share, there is nothing saying they'll actually help
anyone.

-Peter

Oh, sure--but I don't really know how easy it would be to spot and rule
against--what is the difference, really, bewteen organized note sharing
among a given play group and me going out to lunch with Sackett between
rounds and saying "Ooh--Matt had this cool deck with this kinda tech,
and Josh had this cool deck with this kinda tech that killed me..." and
so on?

> There could be some sort of rule against feeding people info outside
> games.

I'm not seeing how it could be even remotely enforcable. There was a
discussion among the Babylon 5 CCG community years ago when the
designers decided to make any sort of scouting at all illegal (as had a
weird system similar to VTES in terms of rounds of multi player games,
but also you could modify your deck between games to an extent, so if
you had information on your opponent's decks at the start of a game,
you had an advantage, as you could modify your deck accordingly),
inventing all sorts of completely absurd rules like how big the play
space had to be (so as to limit how much of the game next to you you
could see) and how when your game was over, you had to essentially put
a bag over your head and stumble out of the play area saying
"yayayayayayay" with your hands over your ears. There was a lot of
discussion over this as it was, understandably, deemed insane. And
eventually, it all just went away (just like the game itself...).

So you *could* try and make rules that limit discussion between people
petween rounds. It just is unlikely to have positive results.

> Yes, there would be lots of grey areas and it could be messy. It
> would certainly require judges to use judgment. It would be worth it in
> my opinion if we started having this secondary game or city rivalries or
> something dumb like that.

Like, I'm not so much seeing how it would make much of a difference
(the share of intel) in any case--you only very rarely see someone's
whole deck. You could very well see a misrepresentation of someone's
deck based on their vampire draw (someone is playing an Arika deck.
They don't draw Arika. They get ousted not to long into the game. They
do well in the other games which no one in your group sees. They are in
the finals, and pull out Arika after you have played a few locations.
You feel dumb.). The difference between painstaking and complicated
note taking and sharing and me discussing the cool decks that ousted me
with Sackett over lunch is a very slim one. And not really worth
worrying about, for my money.

-Peter

That's just talking crap though. There's a world of difference and anyone

I see it like this -

Championship games gather a crowd. It's pretty much the only time vtes
becomes any kind of spectator sport. Observers are supposed to be quiet.
Shouting "No, he's got Archon Investigation!!!" at a critical point of the
game would be seriously bad. Obviously, clearly bad (of course the
observer can't really be penalized in the tournament at that point, but
he'll probably be beaten with sticks). On the other hand, sometimes a
player will do something pretty cool and get some applause, which
technically shouldn't happen. However, everyone understands the audience
isn't attempting to communicate anything critical about the game to that
player. They're just showing appreciation.

Same thing. You sit at a final table with a ream of notes taken by all
your friends. It's clear that you and your friends have gotten together
to try to give you an advantage. You sit at a final table after Sackett
told you that Josh had some really cool tech. No big deal.

We can be sensible and use judgment to tell that one case is problematic
and the other is not.

I appreciate the discussion that people are getting into over this.
There's one aspect of tournament play that hasn't been addressed,
however, and I think this is one area where it's extremely important:
Finals Round seating.

If I am first or second seat going into the finals, quality knowledge
of the other decks could very well spell the difference between winning
and losing the entire tournament, because this is the only time that
players actually get to choose where they sit. The larger the
tournament, the less likely it is that I will have played against the
other decks coming into the final, and therefore the MORE effective a
coordinated intel effort could be. This would be mostly irrelevant if
finals seating were randomized, but I'm not sure anyone wants to go
there. (I would, but I'm not sure anyone else agrees with me.)

-Eric Simon

Specifying the order in which finalists choose their seats sort of
implies that knowledge going into the decision is expected -- selecting
"blind" would be the equivalent of random (barring some metaknowledge,
like never sit next to Tatu or something :-).

If coordinated intel amplifies that, then that's a good thing -- it
reinforces "play to win" by making 1st place that more attractive than
2nd.

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
vol...@yahoo.com wrote:
> If I am first or second seat going into the finals, quality knowledge
> of the other decks could very well spell the difference between winning
> and losing the entire tournament, because this is the only time that
> players actually get to choose where they sit.

This is a situation where, all things being equal, absolute intel is
preferable in all cases to limited intel, in terms of making the game
work better. As you have no control over what decks you do or do not
get to see in the preliminary rounds, and the judges have no control
over whether or not people see a given deck in action by watching a
game after they are ousted or find out about a deck through discussion
over lunch, it would be very significant, as you note, if one player
knew what all the decks in the finals did where another player didn't.
As you have to assume that everyone knows what *some* of the decks in
the finals do (as it is likely in three rounds of a reasonably sized
tournament that you'll play with at least a couple of them), it seems
perfectly reasonable to assume that everyone knows what *all* decks in
the finals do, and then assume that everyone is going to go out of
their way to find out ahead of time.

Trying to restrict this knowledge (by limiting sharing of information
or trying to limit information gathering--see my story about the B5 CCG
up above) is futile. So it seems reasonable to assume that everyone is
going to try to get all of this knowledge, and then not do anything to
try and stop them.

> The larger the
> tournament, the less likely it is that I will have played against the
> other decks coming into the final, and therefore the MORE effective a
> coordinated intel effort could be.

Sure. But it also isn't fair if, by complete chance, one player played
against all 4 other decks in the final, while another player, by
complete chance, played against none of them. The first player would
have a huge advantage in picking a seat, where the second would be at a
significant disadvantage. Granted, this only applies to players seeded
1/2/3 (as 4/5 have no seat choice). So it seems best for everyone to
simply assume everyone has all the information they need, as they could
get it if they tried anyway.

> This would be mostly irrelevant if finals seating were randomized, but I'm not sure >anyone wants to go there.

The final round seating is specifically *not* random to give an
advantage to the top seed going in--if you are first seed, you get to
pick the seat you feel is most advantageous. By design. This assumes
you know what the other decks do. It is likely, in any given
tournament, they you have seen at least a few of the decks in the
final. It is in your best interest to have knowledge of *all* the decks
in the final, and it is really easy to get this information through
checking out other games and talking to firends between rounds. As the
effort needed to prevent this is absurd, it makes perfect sense to set
up a situation where players are assumed to be "scouting" or sharing
intel. As they are going to be doing it anyway.

-Peter

me, each had to win both of the final games, IIRC. Is it playing to win
if I try to get these players ousted as quickly as possible (and
neither is my prey)? I mean, I win the League, but I will probably lose
the game.

matter, but similar situations could arise in other multi-day events.
The results of Day 1 of a Continental Championship don't matter beyond
Qualifying for the next Day, but the impression I get is that the US
Championships will involve some kind of averaging of the results of the
two days, which means that if you get a significant lead, it may be
beneficial to your standing to sabotage someone else's.

Recent Magic major (draft), all in the final group were given
decklists of everyone else's decks specifically to eliminate the
advantage of scouting.

I despise scouting as, even ignoring the unfairness that often arises
out of unequal levels of intel, it punishes decks that run normally
suboptimal plays for their surprise benefits, in turn, leading to
decks being more boring. But, as should be obvious, there's nothing
reasonable that can be done to eliminate scouting.
